query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, phase stability across service-relevant temperatures is governed primarily by the extent of B2-type chemical short-range order (CSRO) on the Al–(Ni,Co) sublattice. Strong negative Al–(Ni,Co) pair interactions lower the free energy by forming B2-like ordered clusters. When the volume fraction and connectivity of these clusters remain below a composition- and temperature-dependent percolation threshold (favored by higher VEC and lower Al activity), the alloy stays as a single-phase FCC matrix with nanoscale B2 CSRO. Once B2 CSRO percolates, a stable two-phase FCC + B2/BCC microstructure forms. Maintaining sub-percolative B2 CSRO stabilizes an FCC matrix that balances high-temperature strength (via order strengthening), environmental resistance (by avoiding Cr depletion into TCP phases), radiation tolerance (via high chemical disorder enabling defect recombination), and cryogenic toughness (via a continuous FCC network).
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, solutionized AlxCoCrFeNi alloys (x in 0.10–0.30, atomic fraction of Al) derived from a Co–Cr–Fe–Ni equiatomic base; grain size >20 µm; random solid solution with minimal prior ordering or precipitates; no detectable TCP phases.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary Al content (e.g., x = 0.10 vs 0.30) and, in a secondary set, adjust Ni/Co to tune VEC at fixed Al. Apply isothermal aging to allow ordering (e.g., 600–800 °C for 10–100 h) without intentional TCP promotion.
generation.conditions: Vacuum induction melted or arc-melted ingots; homogenize at 1150–1200 °C for 24 h, water quench; aging at 700 °C (±50 °C) for 10–100 h in vacuum/inert gas; optional heavy-ion irradiation at 500 °C to ~1 dpa; oxidation exposure in dry air at 900 °C for 100 h; mechanical tests at 77 K and 800 °C under quasi-static loading (strain rate ~10^-3 s^-1).
generation.structural_mediator: The B2 CSRO order parameter and its spatial connectivity (cluster size distribution and percolation across the lattice) within an FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Al exhibits strong negative mixing enthalpies with Ni and Co, driving Al–(Ni,Co) nearest-neighbor bonding and B2-like local ordering. The free-energy reduction from this chemical ordering competes with the configurational entropy and elastic strain energies set by atomic size mismatch and electron concentration (VEC). Higher VEC and lower Al activity suppress long-range order and percolation, keeping B2 CSRO confined to nanoscale clusters embedded in FCC. These clusters strengthen via short-range order strengthening and possibly lower stacking-fault energy moderately without severing the FCC network, thereby retaining cryogenic toughness and radiation defect recombination pathways in the chemically disordered matrix. When B2 CSRO percolates (favored by higher Al and lower VEC), a continuous B2/BCC framework forms, partitioning elements and promoting two-phase stability; this raises high-temperature strength but reduces ductility/toughness and can facilitate Cr partitioning that increases TCP susceptibility under prolonged exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome:
- Composition/structure: At identical aging conditions, Al0.30CoCrFeNi develops a higher B2 CSRO order parameter, larger B2-like cluster sizes, and approaches or crosses a percolation threshold, yielding clear B2 superlattice reflections and/or an FCC + B2/BCC two-phase microstructure; Al0.10CoCrFeNi remains single-phase FCC with only diffuse B2 superlattice scattering from nanoscale CSRO. Increasing VEC at fixed Al reduces the B2 CSRO order parameter and raises the percolation threshold.
- Mechanical: Relative to Al0.10, Al0.30 shows higher yield strength at 800 °C (order-of-magnitude increase expected on the order of tens of percent) but lower uniform elongation, and exhibits markedly reduced cryogenic ductility (e.g., >20–50% drop in uniform elongation) if percolation occurs; Al0.10 maintains high cryogenic work hardening due to FCC matrix continuity with SRO strengthening.
- Radiation: Under identical irradiation, Al0.10 shows smaller and/or fewer defect clusters and lower swelling or hardening increments than Al0.30, consistent with higher chemical disorder and absence of a continuous ordered phase that impedes recombination.
- Environmental resistance: Al0.10 retains Cr in the FCC matrix avoiding TCP; oxidation remains chromia-dominated with stable scales. Al0.30 may shift toward alumina formation; if two-phase forms, any Cr depletion toward TCP is more likely on prolonged exposure than in the single-phase SRO state.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi (no Al): single-phase FCC with negligible B2 CSRO, high cryogenic toughness, relatively lower high-temperature strength, high radiation tolerance; chromia-forming oxidation behavior.
generation.boundary:
- Composition: Al in ~0–0.35 at. fraction; Cr not so high as to independently drive TCP (sigma) under the chosen thermal schedules. Predictions most reliable for near-equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Ni balance.
- Temperature/time: Aging windows where ordering can develop (≈600–800 °C) but prolonged exposures above ~900 °C or very long times may nucleate TCP irrespective of CSRO state.
- Kinetics: Hypothesis addresses thermodynamic stability mediated by CSRO and its percolation; very fast quenching or severe plastic deformation can kinetically suppress ordering and shift observed thresholds.
- Grain size/impurities: Very fine grains or reactive impurities (e.g., C, B) that change boundary energies or promote carbide/boride formation may alter observed phase stability routes.
generation.uncertainty:
- Exact numerical thresholds for VEC and Al content at which percolation occurs depend on minor compositional variations (Ni/Co/Fe ratios), grain size, and defect densities.
- The magnitude of mechanical property changes (percent increases/decreases) will vary with microstructure length scales achieved during aging and irradiation conditions.
- The balance between chromia- vs alumina-dominated scales at higher Al and its interaction with CSRO/percolation is system- and environment-dependent.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloys: Al0.10CoCrFeNi and Al0.30CoCrFeNi (atomic fractions), both homogenized and solutionized identically. Age both at 700 °C for 10, 30, and 100 h. Characterize CSRO and phases, then test mechanical properties at 77 K and 800 °C, irradiate separate specimens at 500 °C to ~1 dpa, and conduct 900 °C/100 h oxidation. In a secondary pair, at fixed Al=0.20, adjust Ni/Co to produce a higher-VEC and a lower-VEC variant and repeat aging and characterization to test VEC control of percolation.
measurements: Synchrotron XRD: presence/intensity of B2 superlattice reflections; diffuse scattering for CSRO quantification
3D atom probe: Al–Ni and Al–Co pair correlation functions; Warren–Cowley SRO parameters vs distance
TEM/SAED and STEM-EDS: identify B2/BCC precipitates, measure cluster/precipitate sizes; assess matrix continuity
SAXS/SANS: cluster size distributions and volume fraction
Tensile tests at 77 K and 800 °C: yield strength, uniform elongation, work hardening rate
Heavy-ion (e.g., 1 MeV Kr) irradiation at 500 °C to ~1 dpa: post-irradiation TEM for defect loop size/density; nanoindentation hardening
Thermogravimetric oxidation at 900 °C in dry air: mass gain kinetics; post-exposure scale composition by XPS/EDS
Optional: Long-term aging at 800–900 °C to check for TCP formation (sigma) by XRD/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following occur: (1) Al0.30 shows equal or lower B2 CSRO order parameter and smaller/less connected B2-like clusters than Al0.10 under identical aging, yet still transforms to FCC + B2/BCC; (2) Al0.10 develops a stable FCC + B2/BCC two-phase microstructure at 700 °C aging while exhibiting low B2 CSRO, indicating percolation is not the mediator; (3) Adjusting VEC at fixed Al does not shift the B2 CSRO level and percolation tendency in the expected direction (higher VEC should suppress percolation), i.e., the higher-VEC variant percolates equally or more than the lower-VEC variant; or (4) Key properties do not correlate with the CSRO/percolation state as predicted—e.g., a percolated B2/BCC state shows equal cryogenic ductility and radiation defect tolerance as a non-percolated CSRO FCC state.
